sections.COMMENTS:
This Individual Source represents the fault activated on 30 October 2016, the largest mainshock of the 2016-17 central Italy seismic sequence (e.g., Chiaraluce et al., 2017; Cirella et al., 2018; Improta et al., 2019; Michele et al., 2020).
This low-angle Source is part of the external frontal and lateral ramp of the Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini (OAS) thrust system inverted and re-activated in the current extensional regime during the 2016-17 Central Italy sequence (Bonini et al., 2019; Buttinelli et al., 2021).
The 2016-17 sequence initiated during the summer of 2016 and includes a succession of moderate to strong extensional earthquakes. These events activated a ca. 70 km long, NNW-SSE trending, multiple fault systems, exhibiting complex ruptures along the backbone of the central Apennines. These events have notoriously and vastly affected the towns of Amatrice, Visso, and Norcia.
The Sibillini Mts. Thrust is the frontal ramp of the OAS and bounds the Apennine mountain front, separating it from the Marche-Abruzzi foothills. This major fault affects the eastern limb of the Mt. Vettore anticline. The Neogene compressional structures have been dissected by NNW-SSE trending Quaternary normal faults, some of which reactivated older extensional structures and do not crosscut the Sibillini Mts. Thrust (Pierantoni et al., 2013).
Historical and instrumental catalogues (ISIDe Working Group, 2007; Guidoboni et al., 2019; Rovida et al., 2021) show a very dense intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) to damaging seismicity within the area. Furthermore, this area of the Apennines has been the locus of numerous destructive earthquakes, including the 12 May 1730 (Mw 6.0) and 22 August 1859 (Mw 5.7) Valnerina events.
This Source results from the extensive studies performed in the area following the 2016-17 seismic sequence (Michele et al., 2016; Chiaraluce et al., 2017; Improta et al., 2019; Michele et al., 2020) and the analysis of the 3D geological model built within the area (Di Bucci et al., 2021).
Various investigators addressed the active tectonics and, subsequently, the seismogenic characteristics of this fault, with widely divergent interpretations. Soon after the largest events of the 2016-17 sequence (24 August, Mw 6.0 and 30 October, Mw 6.5), ground ruptures observed on the Monte Vettore western flank (EMERGEO Working Group, 2016, 2017; Civico et al., 2018; Villani et al., 2018a; Pucci et al., 2021) led to the interpretation of the Monte Vettore - Monte Bove fault system as the causative fault of the 30 October 2016 earthquake (Villani et al., 2018b; Cinti et al., 2019) and to the possible connection of this fault system with the Monti della Laga - Gorzano fault (e.g. Pizzi et al., 2017; Falcucci et al., 2018) responsible for the 24 August 2016 earthquake.
Inversion of strong motion data from the 30 October 2016 earthquake highlighted the contribution to the rupture of the lateral ramp of the OAS thrust system (Scognamiglio et al., 2018). Pizzi et al. (2017) propose that OAS splits the growing normal fault system (Monti della Laga-Gorzano and Monte Vettore - Monte Bove) and acted as a barrier for the 24 August 2016 earthquake, concentrating stress and subsequently initiating the 30 October 2016 rupture (anticipated by the 26 October 2016 event, Mw 5.9).
Focal mechanisms for the 30 October 2016 earthquake and the inversion of GPS and InSAR data suggest that the average dip of the rupture should be at a relatively low angle (ca. 37Â°-38Â°) (Bonini et al., 2019; Cheloni et al., 2019).
Tectonic models for this fault, based on field data and interpretation of seismic reflection profiles, propose the interpretation of the Monte Vettore - Monte Bove as a Quaternary fault system (Porreca et al., 2018, 2020) or as an inherited Mesozoic normal fault transported onto the hangingwall of the Sibillini thrust during the Miocene and later partially reactivated as normal fault during the Quaternary (Bonini et al., 2019; Buttinelli et al., 2021).
The latter interpretation has been confirmed by the comparison between the 3D geological model of the study area (Di Bucci et al., 2021; www.retrace3d.it) and the relocated catalogue of the seismic sequence (Improta et al., 2019; Michele et al., 2020), which showed a strong agreement between the position of the 30 October 2016 mainshock, the aftershocks and the position and geometry of the OAS thrust in this area (Buttinelli et al., 2021). The hypothesis of a link between Quaternary normal faults and inherited thrust faults during the 2016 sequence is further supported by analogue models experiments (Del Ventisette et al., 2021).
This interpretation, a portion of which is represented by this Individual Source, entails that the frontal and lateral ramp of the OAS thrust is currently kinematically inverted and behaves as a normal fault, as earlier suggested (Bonini et al., 2016) by the 24 August 2016 mainshock. The 30 October 2016 earthquake nucleated in the deeper portion of the OAS and involved in the coseismic slip also the Monte Vettore - Monte Bove faults at its hanging-wall.
The reader should notice that this Individual Source is modeled as a single rectilinear rupture, as for any Individual Source anywhere else in the Database, despite the fact that the 30 October 2016 rupture exhibits a complex geometry somehow mimicking the bend of the OAS from its ca. NNW-SSE trending main front to its ca. SW-NE oriented lateral ramp (Bonini et al., 2019). This generalization is due to the current structure of the Database and its constraints in representing Individual Sources as curvilinear geometric elements. The Composite Source enclosing this Individual Source delivers the geometric complexity of this Source inherent to the rupture caused by the 30 October 2016 event.

pictures.t: Geological, seismological, and geodetic data of the 2016-2017 seismic sequence
pictures.c: (a) Semplified geological map, (b) main slip patches of 24 August and 26 October 2016 earthquakes, and (c) coseismic deformation of the 26 October and 30 October 2016 earthquakes (Scognamiglio et al., [2018])

pictures.t: Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini Line, seismogenic sources, and geofluids
pictures.c: Relationships between tectonics and geofluids in the inner Apennines. An alignment of thermal springs and CO2 emissions highlights the presence of the Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini Line (OASL), a major tectonic lineament, that plays a role in controlling the segmentation of seismogenic faults in central Italy (Vannoli et al., [2021]).

pictures.t: Rupture model of the 30 October 2016 earthquake
pictures.c: Rupture model of the 30 October 2016 earthquake by inverting seismograms and GPS data. The model consists of a main normal fault striking N155Â° and dipping 47Â°, and a secondary fault plane striking N210Â° and dipping 36Â°. Updip from the nucleation point, two main slip patches have been imaged on these fault segments, both characterized by similar peak-slip values (~3 m) and rupture times (~3 s)  (Scognamiglio et al., [2018])

pictures.t: Comparison between the slip distributions of the 24 August and the 30 October 2016 earthquakes
pictures.c: Comparison between the slip distributions of the 24 August Amatrice (in red) and the 30 October Norcia (in blue) 2016 main shocks. A slip patch located between the two asperities that ruptured during the 24 August event, just below Accumoli and Arquata del Tronto, demonstrate continuity in the coseismic rupture propagation along and on the single fault plane that ruptured during the first main shock of the sequence (Scognamiglio et al., [2018])

Coseismic surface geological effects following the 30 October Norcia earthquake. 130 researchers of the Open EMERGEO Working Group performed detailed field surveys of the coseismic effects (Villani et al., [2018])
